newsitem.title: USA: Jewish accounts in Swiss banks higher than thought -- source.
newsitem.headline: Jewish accounts in Swiss banks higher than thought -- source.

text.p: The number of unclaimed Holocaust-era Jewish accounts in Swiss banks may be "dramatically higher" than the 774 accounts the Swiss bankers say they have, a source close to the commission probing the issue said on Thursday.
In 1995, the Swiss Bankers Association said 774 such accounts were in its banks with assets of about $32 million.

But the source, who asked not to be identified, said the commission -- headed by former Federal Reserve Bank Chairman Paul Volcker -- had indications that the numbers of accounts were "dramatically higher" than the bankers have admitted.
The Volcker Commission will begin two separate audits of Swiss banks next week, including one to determine if Swiss financial institutions destroyed their Holocaust-era records.

The commission, which consists of three Swiss and three Jewish representatives with Volcker as chairman, agreed to have a pilot audit of of five banks to test procedures for an audit of all Swiss banks later in the year and a "document retention" audit of another five banks to test record-keeping.

The five banks that will be audited in the pilot programme are Credit Suisse, the second largest Swiss bank, the Swiss Bank Corporation, the country's third largest bank, and three smaller banks, Spar und Leihkasse, Banque Cantonale Vaudoise and Picket & Cie.
These banks will be subjected to a forsenic audit to determine the numbers and names of dormant accounts.

Jewish groups maintain that the super-secret Swiss banking system has kept thousands of heirs and survivors from collecting millions of dollars deposited by Jews seeking to avoid Nazi confiscation of their wealth before and during the Holocaust.
Union Bank of Switzerland, the largest Swiss bank, will be one of five banks which will be audited to see if they kept their Holocaust-era records or shredded them.
Last January, a Swiss bank guard reported that Union Bank had been shredding documents from a subsidiary.
The other four banks to be audited to see whether they kept their documents are Banque Baumann, Banque Cantonale de Geneve, Bank Julius Baer and St Gallische Kantonalbank.
The commission, which just wrapped up a meeting in Jerusalem, plans to start work next week on the two audits.

Volcker told a press conference in Geneva on Thursday that the commission expected the names of holders of dormant accounts opened before 1945 to be published in the coming weeks -- including on the Internet.
"We've finally reached the stage of entering into banks," he told a news conference.
"The recommendation of the committee to banking authorities in Switzerland is that a list of names for dormant accounts is to be made available rapidly and to be published," he said.
